title: Humility and the Preservation of the Soul's Powers
english: Having descended from Jerusalem, that is, to Jericho, that is, to the place around the earth and its city called Jericho because of the interpretation of the name—for Jericho is interpreted as moon. And it is said, 'the fool is like the moon, changing,' like a moon which does not have increasing light, but diminishing. And the bride who is being hymned in the Song of Songs, 'emerging beautiful like the dawn' (Song of Songs 6:10), becomes 'like a chosen moon.' This change happens toward the better, toward the perfection; for in one way the moon changes: passing from the moon-like, it comes to the full moon. And there are four transitions of the progress of growth: moon-like, half-moon, quarter-moon, and full moon. And again, from the full moon it comes to the quarter-moon, and from the quarter-moon to the half-moon, and from the half-moon to the moon-like. In this way, the bride of the Word, the perfect soul, the church having been betrothed to him, emerges like the dawn. And she changes so as to become beautiful, chosen like a full moon. And after this he says: 'as a sun, a haze.' And from the lunar light it comes to the solar, being fulfilled of that prophecy which says: 'the moon shall be as the sun' (Malachi 3:1).

Someone, therefore, is being crushed when he is fulfilled of crushed thoughts, of mindsets alien to the healthy thinking of truth. Of these crushings the Savior becomes the physician; for 'he who is being healed' [is] 'those having crushed hearts and binding their fragments,' binding their wounds (Psalm 51:17). And I take by way of an example: someone is crushed many times in a struggle, contending against the adversary, and he attains a crown. Let not these crushings bring him mockery. But when he is crushed by beasts or robbers, we question him—not according to history I say, for he undergoes this through ignorance—but: 'Why has this happened where the beasts are, or why did you approach the spiritual robbers of wickedness?' 'And he will save the lowly in spirit.' Spirit here means the judgment. This is equivalent to that said in the beatitudes of the Gospel: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' (Matthew 5:3), those poor in judgment. These are those who through the Word rightly achieve blindness, those having heard from the Savior saying: 'Learn from me, for I am...'

"I am also humble in heart." But opinion and heart are the same. Just as the Savior is humble in heart, so also those learning from him become humble in opinion. And these are the poor in spirit (Matt 5:3), those who do not wish to be rich in arrogance.

Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and from all their afflictions he will rescue them. It has already been said to us many times that from all of them he rescues (Ps 34:19). 'Many' are 'the afflictions of the righteous'; he said that through life and until a later breath.

The Lord guards all their bones. If they are rescued from all the afflictions so as not to fall and be crushed, all their sustaining powers, called bones, are guarded by God. And it was said before this that the powers of the soul are called its bones; for they are the sustaining powers of the whole soul, while the bones are the sensible powers of the whole body. It was impossible for the flesh or the others to stand; the things sustaining the members of the body are bones.

And the sustaining powers of the soul, such as the mnemonic or the contemplative or the aesthetic of the beautiful, when they are unbending and perfect, are held by God in this, not by their own power. Therefore, they come by preconception toward this willing, but they are perfected according to this, God having cooperated.

Not one of them shall be broken (Ps 34:20). If they are righteous and have cried out to God and were rescued from all the afflictions, 'one' of their bones 'shall not be broken', instead of 'one power'. And that I may begin from the more aesthetic of the powers: there is a certain visual power. When one does not see, so that he may desire the beauty of women and not be conquered by the desire of beauty, this bone was not crushed by the Lord, but is guarded by him harmlessly.

When, having looked into the heaven, one sees the sun and the moon and does not prostrate himself and worship, but from the seen creation understands Him who showed all things, and by analogously contemplating the greatness of His creatures and their beauty, this bone of the sight is strengthened. Thus I take it as more aesthetic, when someone does not accept a vain hearing, but judges by what kind of words he will be persuaded and by what kind not, and by what kind he will agree and by what kind he will be renewed—'compare your ear to the words of the wise', and 'he will not accept a vain hearing'—this one has...

title: Passive vs Active Injustice
english: And the bone, the hearing, the sensation of the hearing, remains uncrushed and healthy. 22 The death of sinners is evil, and those hating the righteous shall suffer lack. For the bones of the righteous are kept by the Lord, and not one of them shall be crushed, but the death of the sinners is evil. It has already been said to us that 'evil' is spoken in two ways. If death, which follows sin, tears one away from the blessed life—according to: 'sin, when completed, brings forth death'—then this death is evil. Again, since they are handed over to punishment having escaped from life, they have died again in order that they might be punished. For it is said: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints'; for how could this be evil, or death be evil, being planted together with the death of Christ? 'For if we are of the same kind,' he says, 'we have become indeed by the likeness of his death, but also of his resurrection.' And: 'If we died with him, we shall also live with him.' 'And those hating the righteous shall suffer lack.' The sinner, if he receives remission of sin, hates the righteous. But hating the righteous, he hates virtue. For the sinners hate the righteous not as a man—for they do not hate the sinners—but as being righteous. But he who hates a physician as a physician, hates the medical art. Because of this they shall suffer lack, they shall be punished.

23 The Lord shall redeem the souls of his servants. Therefore he says: even if an evil death touches the sinners and for those hating the righteous there shall be lack, yet he redeems the good souls of his servants. He redeems the souls from those who previously held them in a painful grip. Again you take it both ways: he is redeemed from punishment and he is redeemed from sin; for if he is redeemed from sin, it follows that he is to be redeemed from punishment. 23 And all those hoping in him shall not suffer lack. All those hoping in God shall not suffer lack like those who suffer lack, namely those hating the righteous; for if for those hating the righteous the lack signifies punishment and penalty, then for those hoping in the Lord, the not suffering lack signifies not being punished, not being penalized, and not falling to those who cause pain.
1 To David. Judge, O Lord, those doing me wrong, fight against those fighting me. No one

He demands a judge, having thoughts as if he were being wronged. It is not the voice of one committing injustice, but rather of one being wronged, rather than one committing injustice. And no one at all prefers being wronged; rather, when both committing injustice and being wronged are set forth, if it is not possible for both to exist—for it is not possible—one chooses rather to be wronged than to commit injustice; for the one committing injustice undergoes punishment, and unrighteous ones are not able to inherit the kingdom of God. But the one being wronged is not tested by these things; for he is being wronged voluntarily. Let us add that even if he is not able to defend himself, he does not exhaust himself in struggle because he cannot take vengeance, but observing what has happened, he sees that the one being wronged is more sympathetic and has many who pity him.

And the unrighteous man, even if no one punishes him, is worthy of punishment. This whole matter of examining injustice and desiring to defend oneself as if one were not committing injustice—his conscience condemns him. There is much boldness for the one saying the psalm: 'Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me, fight against those who fight against me' (Ps 35:23). I do not fight them. And I am 'peaceable among those who hate peace' (Ps 34:14). I am persuaded by the Holy Spirit saying: 'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word: say "our brothers" to those who hate you, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified, but they shall be ashamed' (Isa 54:17).

'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word: say to those who hate you "our brothers"', so that I may speak truly and not merely with a voice; for those saying 'Lord, Lord' with voice alone, He says: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' (Luke 6:46). But the one saying 'in the Holy Spirit' [calls] Lord Jesus, through the participation of the Holy Spirit, by means of those things which he does and thinks; he cries out 'Lord Jesus' according to the Spirit. Therefore, 'say "brothers" to those who hate you'. Let them hate, but you call them brothers truly, not by speech alone, but you act out the obligations due to brothers toward them; for in this way the name of the Lord is glorified; for it is known that someone performs these things through God; for as far as it reaches the hating, he has not spoken of those who hate brothers. 'And they themselves shall be ashamed' (Isa 54:17).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Transformation through Christ's Passion
english: For those who are shamed do not rub [the wound]. Therefore, the saint fights no one. But the one being fought strives not to oppose, but to suffer nothing; and so I shall express it—since it is a violent thing and because of the vividness of the image—that he uses only a weapon, not a sword-shield, nor a defender capable of resisting and opposing.

'Fight those who fight me' (Ps 18:34). There was still in the act of doing wrong to him and in the act of fighting. So that they might no longer do wrong or fight, he asks God for an ally, not so that he might wrong them or fight, but so that he might remain unharmed while being wronged and fought. And the nature of the rational being, if it does not suffer perversion, possesses this as its own characteristic.

'Fight,' therefore, [meaning] prevent them from surrounding me with destruction. Take the weapon and the shield and stand up for my help (Eph 6:16). The shield of God extinguishes the flaming arrows of the enemy, of the evil one. Take therefore this shield, place it around me. I do not say this: 'You shall shield yourself with the shield.' Rather, take it in order to grant it to me, in order to make me secure. The weapon and the shield can be parallel. Perhaps also the kinds of weapons signify [something].

One may pray that the incarnation might happen; for when he takes hold of a man who is able to secure us and fight on our behalf, he took hold of a weapon and a shield and rose for our help. He rose from the bosom of the Father, so that, bending the heavens, he might descend, so that he might be seen fighting on our behalf; for he has come not to fight himself, but to fight on our behalf, and he has come not to suffer simply, but to suffer on our behalf. And behold: 'By the grace of God he has overcome death' (2 Tim 1:10).

We were all under death; our whole race was mortal. And the mortal is subject to death. To say of the one suffering through so much that 'he overcame death.' And that he did not suck up the whole mire of death—for it seems appropriate—thus it was made clear to me also in Isaiah: 'By his wound we were all healed' (Isa 53:5). And his wound, they say, is the cross. Regarding the nature of the cross and the greatness of the injury, it is not a wound. But it is a wound in the sense that, as a wound to him, it is not harming the one possessing it, but benefiting those for whom he bore the wound. So also 'by grace'...

He becomes the righteousness of God through death. For having become in death, he loosed death. And the suffering of the Savior is the loosing of the sufferings; for having become in the sufferings, he loosed them, not being mastered by them.

And just as one becoming a curse looses the curse so as to provide a blessing in its place—for we say he became under a curse not so that he might suffer, but so that he might loose the curse and extend a blessing in its place—so too, he did not make sin for us who did not know sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him (cf. 2 Cor 5:21). Sin becomes the means by which those having righteousness are made righteousness. It is not called sin simply, but sin for the purpose of making those previously mastered by sin righteousness, not simply, but the righteousness of God.

This signifies a participation in the quality; that those who participate are called by the same name as the quality they possess. They possess the quality of the righteousness of God. He conquered so much and mastered so much that not only the unrighteous, but that they might be called righteousness itself. And in many places of the Scripture you will find such things. It says, 'God is love' (1 John 4:8). See the greatness of love: 'God is love' (1 John 4:8). The same essence is signified by both names, God and Love.

Then he says that the one approaching God and loving him with all heart, and with all soul, and with all power, becomes love; for are the things said about love elsewhere—'love does not swell, does not wander, is not unseemly, does not count the evil, covers all, believes all, endures all' (1 Cor 13:4-7)—not things said about virtue? For I do not say that virtue endures or covers or believes. He named the one having love 'love' by the same name. Thus also those holding to righteousness become the righteousness of God from the sin made on our behalf, no longer merely righteous of God but the righteousness of God.

And this signifies perfection, progress. For many of the optative forms in Scripture are presented in the imperative character—perhaps also with others—and so that we may not depart far: 'Hallowed be thy name' (Matt 6:10), which is 'May thy name be hallowed.' 'Thy kingdom come; thy will be done' (Matt 6:10), which is 'May thy will be done.' 'Let the deceitful lips be removed'—instead of...
